Direct-from-China fulfillment can create a real cost advantage, but I would not make it the foundation of a small brand’s US supply chain. The advantage is that qualifying orders valued at $800 or less can generally enter under Section 321 without ordinary duty and formal customs clearance, avoiding not only tariffs but also the cost of importing, warehousing, and fulfilling inventory in the United States. That advantage is meaningful for inexpensive, compact products whose entire customer order stays below the threshold, but it is not a universal exemption because eligibility, product-specific agency requirements, shipment data, and customs limits still apply. Do not model the saving as “the tariff rate times product cost”; compare total delivered cost, including Chinese pick-and-pack fees, parcel postage, air transport, customs-broker or platform fees, payment and foreign-exchange costs, reshipments, refunds, chargebacks, customer-service labor, and the margin lost when delivery is slow. The rule is also a policy risk rather than a permanent competitive advantage, because the $800 threshold and China-specific treatment have been subjects of congressional and trade-policy scrutiny. The material I found does not establish what, if anything, has changed in the Section 321 rules by 24 July 2026, so your broker should confirm the currently effective treatment before you sign a supplier contract. Delivery is the central operational tradeoff: air can move goods from a Chinese factory in roughly days, whereas ocean transport can take a month or more, but air freight is materially more expensive, making a blended air-for-replenishment and ocean-for-base-stock model more practical than sending every unit by premium air. A China-to-customer model also gives you less control over packaging, promised delivery dates, stock accuracy, quality inspection, counterfeit exposure, returns, and replacement orders than inventory held near your customers. The compliance risk is not removed by using a small parcel, a marketplace, a fulfillment intermediary, or Section 321, because the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act applies to goods and components connected wholly or partly to Xinjiang or designated entities and does not provide a de minimis exception for trace amounts. CBP can detain suspected goods, exclude them, or seize and forfeit violating shipments, and release may require a detailed map of the supply chain, supplier identities, production records, bills of materials, invoices, certificates of origin, and transport records. Ordinary supplier certificates or generic social-audit reports may not be enough, because reactive tracing after detention can be slow and expensive and CBP may regard many social-audit programs as lacking independence or credibility. Before importing, require each supplier to disclose factories, subcontractors, raw-material sources, country of origin, HS classifications, bills of materials, labor-risk controls, and records that can be produced quickly to a broker or CBP. For a US warehouse, importing a larger shipment means paying applicable duty and tariffs up front and carrying inventory, but it gives you faster domestic delivery, consolidated freight, easier returns, better quality control, and a more dependable customer experience; a US 3PL adds storage and per-order fees but can substantially reduce the parcel and service friction of China direct shipping. Mexico can be useful for a bonded or near-border fulfillment operation, especially when you want lower-cost regional labor and cross-border parcel processing, but it adds another customs regime, inventory movement, and 3PL relationship rather than eliminating compliance. Canada can similarly provide border-proximate fulfillment and simpler outsourced paperwork, but its apparent tariff benefit should be treated cautiously because a Chinese-made product does not become USMCA-originating merely by being stored or shipped through Canada or Mexico. USMCA duty-free treatment depends on satisfying product-specific rules of origin, so transshipment or warehousing alone does not convert Chinese origin into Mexican or Canadian origin. Implementing policies and procedures to carry out supply chain
due diligence, tracing, management, and documentation is critical
to UFLPA compliance and ensuring that there is no forced labor in
your supply chain.

Assess risks by mapping and then documenting the origin and
method of production at each step in the supply
chain, from the raw materials to the imported product,
including the identity of all entities in the chain and their role
in production.

Institute explicit policies against forced
labor within your company and your supply chain and monitor
compliance.

Collect information about labor conditions in
China, including recruitment methods, wage payment, and
production output per worker.

Implement supply chain management measures to vet
suppliers and terminate relationships
that create risk of exposure to Xinjiang labor while mitigating
impact on workers to the extent possible.

Provide training on forced labor risks for
employees and agents who interact with suppliers.

Conduct comprehensive and independent external
audits to verify implementation and efficacy of policies
and procedures.

Take action to remediate and address any
forced labor identified.

Due to restrictions on information and access in Xinjiang, it
may not be possible for companies to perform full due diligence and
external audits. In such cases, compliance may require use of
alternative technologies and/or termination of contracts with
at-risk suppliers. Companies bear the burden of proving compliance
even when they face barriers to information beyond their
control.

Companies do not have to navigate compliance alone.
Industry-wide initiatives provide additional resources for
companies to responsibly source raw materials such as minerals, cotton, and other products.

Direct-from-China fulfillment can create a real cost advantage, but I would not make it the foundation of a small brand’s US supply chain.

The advantage is that qualifying orders valued at $800 or less can generally enter under Section 321 without ordinary duty and formal customs clearance, avoiding not only tariffs but also the cost of importing, warehousing, and fulfilling inventory in the United States. [shard_00281_7313] [shard_01998_50378]

That advantage is meaningful for inexpensive, compact products whose entire customer order stays below the threshold, but it is not a universal exemption because eligibility, product-specific agency requirements, shipment data, and customs limits still apply. [shard_04647_72515]

Do not model the saving as “the tariff rate times product cost”; compare total delivered cost, including Chinese pick-and-pack fees, parcel postage, air transport, customs-broker or platform fees, payment and foreign-exchange costs, reshipments, refunds, chargebacks, customer-service labor, and the margin lost when delivery is slow.

The rule is also a policy risk rather than a permanent competitive advantage, because the $800 threshold and China-specific treatment have been subjects of congressional and trade-policy scrutiny. [shard_00281_7313] [shard_01256_1845]

The material I found does not establish what, if anything, has changed in the Section 321 rules by 24 July 2026, so your broker should confirm the currently effective treatment before you sign a supplier contract.

Delivery is the central operational tradeoff: air can move goods from a Chinese factory in roughly days, whereas ocean transport can take a month or more, but air freight is materially more expensive, making a blended air-for-replenishment and ocean-for-base-stock model more practical than sending every unit by premium air. [shard_02554_10664]

A China-to-customer model also gives you less control over packaging, promised delivery dates, stock accuracy, quality inspection, counterfeit exposure, returns, and replacement orders than inventory held near your customers.

The compliance risk is not removed by using a small parcel, a marketplace, a fulfillment intermediary, or Section 321, because the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act applies to goods and components connected wholly or partly to Xinjiang or designated entities and does not provide a de minimis exception for trace amounts. [shard_04073_1206] [shard_02843_75195]

CBP can detain suspected goods, exclude them, or seize and forfeit violating shipments, and release may require a detailed map of the supply chain, supplier identities, production records, bills of materials, invoices, certificates of origin, and transport records. [shard_04073_1206]

Ordinary supplier certificates or generic social-audit reports may not be enough, because reactive tracing after detention can be slow and expensive and CBP may regard many social-audit programs as lacking independence or credibility. [shard_05416_9280]

Before importing, require each supplier to disclose factories, subcontractors, raw-material sources, country of origin, HS classifications, bills of materials, labor-risk controls, and records that can be produced quickly to a broker or CBP.

For a US warehouse, importing a larger shipment means paying applicable duty and tariffs up front and carrying inventory, but it gives you faster domestic delivery, consolidated freight, easier returns, better quality control, and a more dependable customer experience; a US 3PL adds storage and per-order fees but can substantially reduce the parcel and service friction of China direct shipping. [shard_00930_22193]

Mexico can be useful for a bonded or near-border fulfillment operation, especially when you want lower-cost regional labor and cross-border parcel processing, but it adds another customs regime, inventory movement, and 3PL relationship rather than eliminating compliance. [shard_04647_72515]

Canada can similarly provide border-proximate fulfillment and simpler outsourced paperwork, but its apparent tariff benefit should be treated cautiously because a Chinese-made product does not become USMCA-originating merely by being stored or shipped through Canada or Mexico. [shard_06034_48344] [shard_04462_49533]

USMCA duty-free treatment depends on satisfying product-specific rules of origin, so transshipment or warehousing alone does not convert Chinese origin into Mexican or Canadian origin. [shard_04462_49533]

My practical recommendation is a hybrid: keep slow-moving, experimental, very low-value, non-regulated items in direct China fulfillment only after a broker validates classification and documentation; hold proven bestsellers and anything needed quickly in a US 3PL; and test Mexico or Canada only when measured cross-border savings exceed their extra handling, customs, and inventory costs.

Require the supplier or platform to provide a written landed-cost quote, service-level commitment, tracking and returns process, product-safety documentation, forced-labor records, and a contingency plan for a rejected or detained parcel before moving meaningful volume.

If a supplier’s pitch depends mainly on “everyone stays under $800” and cannot explain origin, HS codes, factory traceability, returns, and what happens if Section 321 treatment changes, the apparent saving is probably regulatory arbitrage rather than a durable supply-chain advantage.
